promptText: What best captures the philosophy behind "progressive" in Progressive Web App?
options: The app works at a baseline for every visitor and progressively enhances itself with installability, reliability, speed, and engagement as the platform allows
A PWA must be entirely rewritten from scratch using a special PWA-only framework, distinct from a normal web app
"Progressive" refers only to progressive JPEG-style image loading on the page
PWAs only function correctly in Chrome and are not built on open web standards
explanation: A PWA is not a different kind of app but a normal web app that earns installable, reliable, fast, and engaging properties by adopting a small set of web platform APIs on top of what's already shipped.

promptText: A developer adds a valid manifest.json but sees no install prompt appear. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: A registered service worker with a fetch handler that returns a real 200 response for the start URL, served over HTTPS — the manifest alone doesn't trigger installability
The manifest's icons must be in SVG format rather than PNG for the browser to recognize them
The app must first be packaged as a native binary and submitted to an app store
manifest.json must be renamed to app.json for the browser to detect it
explanation: Chrome's install heuristic requires the manifest, a registered service worker whose fetch handler produces a real 200 response for the start URL, and HTTPS — a manifest by itself does nothing visible.

promptText: Which statement about a service worker is accurate?
options: It runs on its own thread with no DOM access, and the browser can spin it down and wake it up per event at will
It shares the page's JavaScript execution context and can directly call document.querySelector
It persists in memory permanently and the browser never terminates or restarts it
It gains DOM access automatically once it reaches the activate lifecycle stage
explanation: A service worker runs on a separate thread with no DOM access at all, and every handler must be self-contained and idempotent because the browser can terminate and restart the worker between events.

promptText: Which caching strategy is best suited for content-hashed, versioned static assets that never change once fetched?
options: Cache-first
Network-first
Network-only
Stale-while-revalidate is strictly worse than network-only for this exact case
explanation: If the bytes at a URL never change, cache-first (check cache, only hit network on a miss) is ideal — there's no reason to ever re-fetch content that's guaranteed immutable.

promptText: Why is navigator.onLine not a reliable way to decide whether a fetch will actually succeed?
options: It only reflects whether the OS reports a network interface as connected — a device can report "online" while stuck behind a captive portal with no real route out
navigator.onLine always returns true regardless of the device's actual connection state
navigator.onLine only functions correctly after a service worker has been registered
The API is deprecated and no longer implemented by any modern browser
explanation: navigator.onLine is a useful UX signal but not authoritative — the real source of truth for whether a request will succeed is the fetch itself succeeding or failing, not the connectivity flag.

promptText: Why do browsers require HTTPS (with a localhost exception) to register a service worker?
options: A service worker can intercept and rewrite every response in its scope, so allowing registration over plain HTTP would give a network attacker a persistent, silent man-in-the-middle position
HTTPS is required purely to satisfy app-store submission checklists, unrelated to browser security
Service workers consume significantly more bandwidth, so HTTPS compression is mandated to offset it
It is an arbitrary legacy restriction from early browser implementations with no current security rationale
explanation: A service worker delivered over a compromised HTTP connection would hand an attacker a persistent, silent request-rewriting position that survives page reloads — far more dangerous than a single injected script.

promptText: Calling self.skipWaiting() and clients.claim() unconditionally makes service worker updates apply immediately. What real risk does this introduce?
options: It can pull the rug out from under a user mid-interaction, since a request in flight could suddenly be served by different worker logic/cache mid-session, which is exactly what the default waiting phase is designed to prevent
It permanently disables the fetch event handler for all future page loads
It causes the manifest.json file to become invalid and rejected by the browser
It prevents the service worker from ever being updated again in the future
explanation: The default waiting phase exists so a page never has old JS talking to a new cache (or vice versa) mid-session; skipWaiting/clients.claim are deliberate escape hatches with a real consistency tradeoff, not defaults.

promptText: A team adds skipWaiting() and clients.claim() to "make updates apply faster," but their cache name never changes between deploys. What actually happens?
options: Every open tab is forced onto the new worker sooner, but since the cache name never changed, it just takes over serving the same stale cached assets faster — making the stale-bundle problem worse, not better
The stale-bundle problem is fully solved, because skipWaiting forces a fresh network fetch of every cached asset
The browser automatically detects the missing cache-name bump and deletes the old cache on its own
Nothing changes at all, because skipWaiting has no effect without also restarting the browser process
explanation: skipWaiting/clients.claim control when the new worker takes over, not what it serves — without fixing cache versioning first, forcing faster takeover just delivers the same stale cache to users sooner.

promptText: How does Workbox's build-time precache manifest structurally prevent the classic "stale JS bundle forever" bug?
options: It computes a content hash per asset so a changed file is guaranteed to get a new cache entry/URL, instead of relying on a developer remembering to bump a cache version name
Workbox disables browser caching entirely for all JavaScript files across the application
Workbox re-fetches every single asset over the network on every page load regardless of any cache
Workbox requires the end user to manually clear their browser cache before every deploy
explanation: Workbox's build plugin injects a revisioned manifest so a code change is structurally guaranteed to produce a new cache entry, replacing the error-prone practice of manually bumping a cache name on every deploy.

promptText: Why can't a production app rely solely on the Background Sync API to guarantee a queued offline POST eventually completes?
options: Background Sync has inconsistent browser support (notably long missing in Safari/Firefox), so it needs a feature-detected fallback such as retrying the request on the next app load
Background Sync only works for GET requests and structurally cannot queue a POST
Background Sync requires the tab to remain open continuously, which defeats its own purpose
Background Sync has been fully deprecated in favor of raw WebSocket connections
explanation: Background Sync is a Chromium feature with real support gaps elsewhere, which is why it's typically used as a progressive enhancement (often via Workbox's durable queue) on top of a working retry-on-next-launch baseline.

promptText: Why can a push notification be delivered and shown even when the site's tab is completely closed?
options: The browser vendor's own push service (not the page) receives the push message from the server and wakes the service worker, which then calls the Notifications API to display it
The browser silently keeps a hidden tab open in the background indefinitely for every subscribed site
Push notifications are actually delivered as SMS messages as a fallback delivery mechanism
The operating system polls the server every second to check for new messages, even with the browser fully closed
explanation: The Push API and Notifications API are two separate pieces: the browser's push service delivers the message and wakes the service worker independent of any open tab, and the worker then displays the notification via a separate API.

promptText: What is the key functional difference between the Cache API (used by service workers) and IndexedDB?
options: The Cache API stores full Request/Response pairs optimized for replaying HTTP responses, while IndexedDB stores structured, queryable JavaScript objects optimized for reading and filtering data
The Cache API and IndexedDB are functionally identical and fully interchangeable in every use case
IndexedDB can only store plain strings, exactly like localStorage, with no structured data support
The Cache API supports SQL-style queries across stored responses, while IndexedDB does not support querying at all
explanation: A mature PWA typically uses both together: the Cache API for replaying assets/API responses byte-for-byte, and IndexedDB for structured domain data and write queues that need to be actually queried, not just replayed.

promptText: A team's service worker uses importScripts() to pull in a shared utility file that changes on every deploy but carries no cache-busting hash. What subtle staleness bug can this cause, even though sw.js itself is correctly re-fetched on every navigation?
options: Unlike the top-level sw.js file, scripts loaded via importScripts() are not automatically exempt from HTTP caching, so the browser can serve a stale cached copy of the imported script even while correctly detecting that sw.js itself changed
importScripts() files are always cached forever with no possible fix regardless of headers used
importScripts() only executes once per browser installation and is never re-evaluated on subsequent deploys
sw.js and every script it imports are always byte-diffed together as a single atomic unit, making this scenario impossible
explanation: The top-level service worker script is deliberately exempt from HTTP caching for its update check, but files pulled in via importScripts() don't automatically get that exemption — they need their own cache-busting (a hash in the URL) to avoid being served stale.

promptText: A service worker script is served from /scripts/sw.js but the team wants it to control the entire site at /. What must they do, and why doesn't the browser allow this by default?
options: The server must send a Service-Worker-Allowed header explicitly naming the broader scope, because without that opt-in, one arbitrary path on a site could unilaterally claim control over unrelated parts of the same origin
Scope is determined entirely by a field inside manifest.json, and the service worker script's own file path is irrelevant to scope
Any registered service worker automatically controls the entire origin regardless of where its script file is hosted
Scope can only be widened by physically moving the script file to the domain's root directory; there is no header-based option
explanation: A service worker defaults to controlling only paths at or below its own script location, and widening that requires an explicit Service-Worker-Allowed header — preventing one part of a site from silently taking over another.

promptText: A PWA passes every Lighthouse installability check (valid manifest, registered service worker, HTTPS) but users still describe the app as janky and slow. What does this reveal about what the installability checklist actually measures?
options: Installability checks only verify the technical criteria for the install prompt to fire — they say nothing about actual runtime performance, which is instead captured separately by Core Web Vitals like LCP, CLS, and INP
Lighthouse's installability score and its Core Web Vitals score are mathematically the same metric expressed under different names
Passing every installability check guarantees a perfect Core Web Vitals score by definition
Lighthouse stopped evaluating PWAs entirely starting with version 10, so this result is expected and meaningless
explanation: Installability criteria gate whether beforeinstallprompt can fire at all; they're a separate concern from Core Web Vitals, which is why a technically-installable PWA can still fail the "fast" and "reliable" pillars if it performs poorly.
